entities.name: Adalbert of Mainz
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adalbert of Mainz (c. 1060–1137) was Archbishop of Mainz from 1111 to 1137 and one of the most politically consequential churchmen of the Investiture Controversy's climax and resolution. A close confidant of Emperor Henry V, he was nonetheless a driving force in the negotiations that produced the Concordat of Worms (1122) — the compromise settlement that officially ended the Investiture Controversy.

Adalbert's career illustrates the extraordinary complexity of the Investiture Controversy's final phase. He served as Henry V's chancellor and was closely associated with the emperor, even accompanying him to Rome in 1111 when Henry briefly imprisoned Pope Paschal II. Yet Adalbert was also connected to the reform party, and he eventually emerged as one of the architects of the compromise that distinguished spiritual investiture (with ring and staff, reserved to the Church) from temporal investiture (with sceptre, retained by the empire).

As Archbishop of Mainz — the primacy of all Germany — his support for the Concordat of Worms carried enormous institutional weight. Mainz was the most prestigious German see, with the right to crown German kings, and its archbishop's signature on the concordat was essential to its validity. Adalbert's role in ending the Investiture Controversy made him one of the most consequential German churchmen of his century.
